title: De Fide Orthodoxa
author: Phoebaudus Aginnensis Episcopus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp351.tmp351.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Videtis ergo omnia eos in tractatu ipsorum, non evangelica tide, sed subdola malignitate ad seducen- dos simplices quosque posuisse. Non jam tam sus- pectum, quam manifestum omnibus esse debet, ita eos Deum de Deo posuisse, ut Arius tradere solebat, ut ex Deo factus sit, non ex Deo natus. Qui si natus est, unius substantiae est : si factus est, verus Filius non est : et si verus Filius non est, nec verus Deus est : aut si verus Deus est, et de Patre non est, duo sunt habentes singuli et voluntates proprias, et imperia diversa : vel si concordia tantum et socie- tate unum sunt, non tamen et substantia verus, ut jam dixi, Deus non est.
passages.english: You see, then, that in their treatise they have set down everything not in evangelical faith but with crafty malice, to lead astray all the simple-minded. It ought now to be not so much suspected as plain to everyone that they have set down "God from God" in the way Arius used to teach, namely that he was made from God, not born from God. If he was born, he is of one substance; if he was made, he is not the true Son; and if he is not the true Son, neither is he true God; or, if he is true God and is not from the Father, there are two, each having both his own will and a separate rule; or, if they are one only by agreement and fellowship, and not also in substance, then, as I have already said, he is not true God.
passages.notes: "tide" is a scanning error for "fide" (faith). The final clause is compressed in the Latin. Taken literally, "non tamen et substantia verus ... Deus non est" is awkward. It is translated here as "not also in substance, [then] he is not true God".

passages.original: Ita et Fi- lium Dei similem volunt, ut eum aliunde similem, non de ipsa una sancta et beata Patris substantia dicant. Qui si de Patris substantia non est, «vx ό'ντων est, id est, ex nullis exstantibus, ut idem Arius tradidit : sublato enim eo quod Pater est, undecum- que fuerit Filius, necesse est ut et initium ex nihilo, et ortum ex tempore habeat : nihil enim sine initio, nisi solus Deus.
passages.english: So too they want the Son of God to be "like", in such a way that they say he is like from some other source, and not from the one holy and blessed substance of the Father itself. If he is not from the Father's substance, he is *ex ouk ontōn*, that is, from things not existing, as the same Arius taught. For once what the Father is has been taken away, wherever the Son came from, he must necessarily have both a beginning from nothing and an origin in time; for nothing is without beginning except God alone.
passages.notes: The Greek is garbled in the scan ("«vx ό'ντων"). It is evidently ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων ("from things not existing"), the Arian formula, and the Latin gloss that follows confirms this.
